resources.string: Winning tips
Quick ideas you can use in your very next game
Each tip takes about 30 seconds. Pick one idea, try it in your next game, and come back when it starts to feel natural.
Basics
Step up
Expert level
These are easier to understand after the earlier tips feel natural. You can read them anytime, but there is no need to learn them first.
For your next game
Previous
Next
Do not grab too many discs early
More discs does not always mean a better position.
Early in the game, flipping many discs can expose more edges of your own discs and give your opponent useful choices. A quiet move that flips only a little can be easier to control.
Do not automatically choose the move that flips the most discs.
The outlined move flips only one disc. The × move flips four, but taking more is not automatically better.
Reduce your opponent’s choices
A strong move often leaves the opponent with fewer places to play.
Instead of asking only how many discs you flip, look at what the opponent can do next. In this example the outlined move leaves much less freedom than the × move.
Before you play, ask: “How many moves will they have after this?”
Outlined: the opponent gets 4 legal moves. ×: the opponent gets 9.
Corners are very strong
A disc in a corner can never be flipped.
Corners are special because nothing can surround them from outside the board. Taking one often gives you a stable base for the nearby edge as well.
When a corner is available, check it before looking elsewhere.
The outlined corner is a legal move in this position.
Be careful next to an empty corner
The diagonal square beside a corner can hand that corner to your opponent.
The diagonal square next to a corner is often called an X-square. It is not always bad, but playing there without checking can make the corner immediately available to the opponent.
Before playing diagonally beside an empty corner, check whether the opponent can take the corner next.
Playing the × at b2 makes the outlined a1 corner available to the opponent.
Do not rush to the edge
An edge looks safe, but taking it too early can make the position harder to control.
Edge discs are harder to flip than interior discs, but they are not automatically stable. Early edge moves can create access to corners or force you into awkward follow-up moves.
Do not choose a move just because it reaches the edge.
The × move reaches the edge. The outlined interior move is worth comparing first.
In the endgame, count discs again
The goal changes as the board fills up: the final disc count now matters directly.
Early on, mobility matters more than the current score. With only a few empty squares left, start comparing how many discs each sequence can leave you with at the end.
When the empty spaces become few, switch from “stay flexible” to “how does this finish?”
Only 10 empty squares remain. The outlined move is one of the large-flip candidates to compare.
Notice discs that can no longer flip
Stable discs are points you can rely on until the game ends.
A corner disc is always stable. From a secured corner, connected edge discs can also become stable. Learning to notice these discs makes the final score easier to estimate.
After someone takes a corner, look along the connected edges for discs that may already be safe.
The outlined corner has already been taken, so that disc can never flip again.
Parity: look at even and odd empty regions
This is an expert idea. Near the end, who gets the last move in a region can matter a lot.

When empty squares split into small regions, count how many squares each region has. Even and odd regions interact with whose turn it is, passes, and move order. Use this only after the earlier endgame ideas feel comfortable.
Start simply: when the board is nearly full, notice whether an isolated empty region has an even or odd number of squares.
The outlined top-right region has 2 empty squares: an even-sized region.
Count remaining moves, not only discs
Another expert habit is to estimate how many useful moves each side can still make.

In a tight endgame, a move can be valuable because it changes who is forced to enter a region first. Counting the remaining empty squares and likely move order is the bridge from simple endgame play to deeper reading.
With only a few spaces left, count the likely moves before choosing the move that flips the most right now.
The outlined empty squares are useful checkpoints when counting the remaining move order.
